intro: Games once belonged to one town, one temple or one school. This unit follows two ways they became bigger. The first is the Olympic Games. A festival at Olympia in Greece became, after 1894, a stage where nations march behind flags. Federations wrote shared codes so athletes from different countries could meet under one set of rules.

The second is a law. Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972 is one sentence about education. It never names a sport. Yet it changed who gets a spot on a school team. In Illinois, the IHSA crowned its first boys wrestling champions in 1937 and held its first girls wrestling state finals in 2022.

In this unit you will read dates, laws, court cases and records. You will be able to explain who wrote a rule, who was shut out and when a door opened. You will also be able to weigh an argument, like whether a country should boycott the Games.
bigQuestion: Who decides who gets a place on the roster, and how do flags, codes and laws change that answer?

title: Nations and New Rosters

chapters.title: Olympics as a Stage
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a festival at one Greek sanctuary become a stage where nations meet, argue and sometimes stay away?

story.title: A Flag Over a Borrowed Stadium
story.kicker: For about two weeks, a city lends its biggest room to the world.
paragraphs: Summer, 1984. The Los Angeles Memorial Coliseum is full. The same stadium held the Olympic Games in 1932. Tonight it holds them again. Teams walk in one by one behind their flags. Each team carries a sign with its country's name.

A white flag climbs a pole at one end of the stadium. It shows five rings: blue, yellow, black, green and red. Pierre de Coubertin designed that flag in 1913. It first flew at the Games in Antwerp, Belgium, in 1920.

Some flags are missing tonight. The Soviet Union and more than a dozen allied countries have stayed home. Four years earlier, the United States led a boycott of the Moscow Games. Each boycott was a message sent with an empty place in the parade.

The Coliseum does not belong to the Olympics. It belongs to Los Angeles. When the Games end, the rings flag comes down and is handed to the next host city. The stadium goes back to football, concerts and graduations.

A student in the stands reads the program. It lists sports, events and national teams. Every event runs on a rule book written by an international federation. The student wonders who wrote all these rules, and why so many countries agreed to them.
story.think: Why might a country choose to stay away from the Games instead of coming and losing?

lessons.title: A Festival for Zeus
lessons.mainIdea: The ancient Olympic Games were a religious festival at Olympia, open to freeborn Greek men, held every four years for more than a thousand years.
reading: *Olympia* is a sanctuary in the western Peloponnese, in southern Greece. A sanctuary is a holy place. Olympia was sacred to Zeus, the chief Greek god. Greek tradition dates the first Games there to 776 BCE. Historians treat that date as a tradition, not a proven record.

The festival came every four years. Greeks called that four-year span an *Olympiad* and sometimes used it to count time. The oldest event was the stadion, a footrace about 192 meters long. Later came boxing, wrestling, the pentathlon and chariot races. A truce asked travelers to be let through safely to the festival.

Only freeborn Greek men could compete. Enslaved people and foreigners were shut out. The writer Pausanias says married women were barred from watching. Yet Kyniska, a Spartan princess, is listed as a winner in 396 and 392 BCE. She owned the winning chariot horses, and owners were counted as victors.

The Games lasted into the time of the Roman Empire. Christian emperors in the late 300s CE banned the old festivals for the gods. The Games are often said to end around 393 CE, though historians debate the exact year. German archaeologists began digging up Olympia in 1875.

words.d: a sanctuary of Zeus in southern Greece where the ancient Games were held
the four-year span between one Olympic Games and the next
a holy place set aside for worship of a god

look.title: An Owner Who Won

lessons.title: Coubertin's Congress
lessons.mainIdea: In June 1894, a meeting at the Sorbonne in Paris founded the International Olympic Committee and planned new Games.
reading: Pierre de Coubertin was a French educator born in 1863. He admired sport in English schools such as Rugby School. In 1890 he visited the Wenlock Olympian Games in England. A doctor named William Penny Brookes had started those local games in 1850.

Other people had also used the Olympic name. A Greek donor, Evangelis Zappas, paid for Olympic contests in Athens in 1859 and 1870. The digs at ancient Olympia drew public interest too. Coubertin wanted something bigger: Games that moved between nations.

In June 1894, Coubertin gathered a *congress* at the Sorbonne, a university in Paris. A congress is a formal meeting of delegates. On June 23, 1894, it founded the *International Olympic Committee*, or *IOC*. Demetrios Vikelas of Greece became its first president. The congress chose Athens for the first Games, in 1896.

the body founded in 1894 that runs the Olympic Games
short for International Olympic Committee

lessons.title: Athens, 1896
lessons.mainIdea: The first modern Olympic Games were held in Athens in April 1896, in a rebuilt ancient stadium, with only men competing.
reading: The first modern Games opened in Athens in April 1896. The main site was the *Panathenaic Stadium*, an ancient stadium rebuilt in marble. A wealthy Greek merchant, George Averoff, paid for the rebuilding. The stadium still stands today.

About 240 athletes took part, from 14 nations, by common counts. All of them were men. Many were students or members of clubs, not national teams chosen by trials. James Connolly of the United States won the triple jump, the first final of the Games.

Winners received a silver medal and an olive branch. The gold, silver and bronze pattern began later, at the 1904 Games. The new *marathon* race ran from the town of Marathon to Athens. It was based on a legend of a messenger running from a battle. A Greek runner, Spyridon Louis, won it.

a long road race first held at the 1896 Games, named for the Greek town of Marathon

lessons.title: Women Enter in 1900
lessons.mainIdea: Women first competed in the Olympics at the 1900 Paris Games, and their events grew slowly over the next century.
reading: The 1900 Games took place in Paris as part of a World's Fair. Events were spread over several months. For the first time, women competed. By common counts, 22 women took part among about a thousand athletes.

Charlotte Cooper of Britain won the women's tennis singles in July 1900. She became the first woman to win an individual Olympic event. Women also played golf in Paris. Coubertin himself did not favor women competing, but the Paris organizers added some events.

Growth came event by event. Women's track and field joined the program at Amsterdam in 1928. The women's marathon was first held at Los Angeles in 1984. At the 2012 London Games, every nation sent at least one woman for the first time. Saudi Arabia, Qatar and Brunei sent women that year.

lessons.title: Federations Write the Rules
lessons.mainIdea: International federations, many founded in the early 1900s, keep one rule book for each sport so athletes from different nations can meet.
reading: Before the 1900s, the same sport often had different rules in different countries. Two teams could arrive at a match and disagree about the rules. An *international federation* fixes that. It is a body that writes one set of rules for one sport, worldwide.

Soccer's federation, *FIFA*, was founded in Paris in May 1904. The swimming federation began in London in 1908 and is now called World Aquatics. The track and field federation began in Stockholm in 1912 and is now World Athletics. Basketball's federation, FIBA, was founded in Geneva in 1932.

The IOC does not write the rules for each event. Each federation runs its own sport at the Games. A federation's rule book is a *code*: a written set of rules everyone agrees to follow. A code flattens local differences so a runner from Kenya and a runner from Chicago race under the same rules.

the international federation for soccer, founded in Paris in 1904
a written set of rules that everyone in a sport agrees to follow

lessons.title: Games In and Out
lessons.mainIdea: The Olympic program has added and dropped sports over time, so some local games reached the world stage and others left it.
reading: The list of Olympic sports keeps changing. Tug of war was an Olympic event from 1900 to 1920. Lacrosse, a game first played by Native nations in North America, was on the program in 1904 and 1908. Cricket was played only once, in 1900, when Britain beat France.

Basketball joined the Olympics at Berlin in 1936. The games were played outdoors. James Naismith, who invented the game in 1891, was there to watch. Judo joined at Tokyo in 1964 for men. It was the first Olympic sport to come from Japan. Women's judo was added in 1992.

A sport must have an international federation recognized by the IOC to be on the program. Host cities may also propose sports. For the 2028 Games in Los Angeles, the IOC approved cricket, lacrosse and flag football in 2023. Old games can return when their federations grow strong.

lessons.title: The Amateur Rule
lessons.mainIdea: For most of the 1900s, Olympic rules barred athletes who had been paid for sport, and the rule cost Jim Thorpe his medals.
reading: Early Olympic leaders wanted only *amateurs*. An amateur is someone who is not paid to play. The rule favored people who could afford to train without a sports income. Workers who earned money from sport could be shut out.

*Jim Thorpe* was a member of the Sac and Fox Nation. At the 1912 Stockholm Games, he won gold in both the pentathlon and the decathlon. In 1913, newspapers reported he had been paid to play minor-league baseball in 1909 and 1910. His medals were taken away.

The IOC restored his medals in 1982, after his death, naming him a co-champion. In 2022, the IOC listed him as the only champion in both events. Over the 1970s and 1980s, the IOC let federations decide who could compete. At Barcelona in 1992, NBA players joined the U.S. basketball team.

sections.title: Rings, Flags and a Rented Stage

lessons.title: Symbols With Birth Dates
lessons.mainIdea: Olympic symbols such as the rings, the oath, the flame and the torch relay were each added at a known date in the 1900s.
reading: Olympic *symbols* can feel ancient, but most are modern. The motto Citius, Altius, Fortius means "faster, higher, stronger" in Latin. It was adopted in 1894. In 2021, the IOC added a fourth word, Communiter, meaning "together."

Coubertin designed the five-ring flag in 1913. The rings are blue, yellow, black, green and red on white. Coubertin wrote that these colors, with the white, could build the flag of every nation of his time. The flag first flew at Antwerp in 1920. An athlete also spoke the first Olympic oath there.

A flame burned at the Amsterdam Games in 1928. The torch relay from Olympia to the host city began in 1936, for the Berlin Games. The Nazi government used that relay for propaganda. The relay has been held ever since, but its first use reminds us that symbols serve whoever holds them.

words.d: an object or sign that stands for an idea
a short saying that sums up a group's aims
the carrying of a flame from Olympia to the host city, first done in 1936

lessons.title: Teams Under Flags
lessons.mainIdea: Athletes enter the Games through National Olympic Committees, so they march under flags, even though the IOC's charter says the Games are contests between athletes.
reading: Each country sends its team through a *National Olympic Committee*, or NOC. The IOC recognizes each NOC. Today there are more than 200. The number of teams grew as empires broke up and new nations formed, especially after 1945.

The IOC's rule book is called the *Olympic Charter*. It says the Games are contests between athletes, not between countries. Yet athletes march behind flags, and anthems play at medal ceremonies. Newspapers often print medal tables that rank nations. The charter and the flags pull in two directions.

Sometimes athletes compete without a national flag. In 1992, athletes from Yugoslavia, then under United Nations sanctions, entered as Independent Olympic Participants. At Rio de Janeiro in 2016, ten athletes formed the first Refugee Olympic Team. They marched under the Olympic flag.

words.d: the body in each country that enters its athletes in the Games
the IOC's written rule book for the Olympic movement
a person forced to leave their home country

lessons.title: A City Rents the Stage
lessons.mainIdea: The IOC owns the Games but not the stadiums, so a host city builds or lends its venues and carries the cost.
reading: IOC members vote to choose a *host city*. The city signs a contract with the IOC. It provides stadiums, pools, housing and transport. The Games last about two weeks. Then the venues go back to the city, and the bills stay there too.

Chicago won the vote for the 1904 Games. The Games were then moved to St. Louis, to join the Louisiana Purchase Exposition, a World's Fair. Much later, Chicago bid for the 2016 Games. On October 2, 2009, IOC members met in Copenhagen. Chicago was eliminated in the first round, and Rio de Janeiro won.

Costs can last for decades. Montreal built a large stadium for the 1976 Games. Quebec finished paying off that stadium debt in 2006. Los Angeles took another path in 1984. It reused the Coliseum from 1932 and other existing buildings. Those Games ended with a surplus.

words.d: the city chosen to hold an Olympic Games
a city's formal offer to host the Games
money left over after all costs are paid

lessons.title: Berlin, 1936
lessons.mainIdea: Americans argued about boycotting the 1936 Berlin Games because Nazi Germany excluded Jewish athletes, but the U.S. team went.
reading: The IOC gave the 1936 Summer Games to Berlin in 1931. In 1933, Adolf Hitler and the Nazi Party took power in Germany. The Nazi government pushed Jewish athletes out of German sports clubs. Many people abroad asked whether other nations should attend.

In the United States, a *boycott* movement grew. A boycott is a refusal to take part, used as a protest. Jeremiah Mahoney, head of the Amateur Athletic Union, favored a boycott. Avery Brundage, head of the American Olympic Committee, opposed it. In December 1935, the Amateur Athletic Union voted narrowly to send athletes.

Germany named one athlete of Jewish descent to its team, the fencer Helene Mayer. She won a silver medal. Jesse Owens, a Black American, won four gold medals in Berlin. At home in the United States, Owens still faced segregation. The 1936 Games showed that a host can use the stage for its own message.

words.d: a refusal to take part in something, used as a protest
messages spread to make people support a government or cause
Black American athlete who won four gold medals at Berlin in 1936

look.title: Two Leaders, One Vote
look.text: Jeremiah Mahoney argued that going to Berlin would support a government that shut out Jewish athletes. Avery Brundage argued that sport should stay apart from politics and the athletes should go. The Amateur Athletic Union voted in December 1935. The side that wanted to go won by a small margin.
look.prompt: Pick one side. What is the strongest reason for it, and what would the other side say back?

lessons.title: Boycotts in the Cold War
lessons.mainIdea: From 1956 to 1984, countries and blocs stayed away from the Games to protest wars, invasions and apartheid in South Africa.
reading: In 1956, Melbourne, Australia, hosted the Games. The Netherlands, Spain and Switzerland stayed away after the Soviet Union invaded Hungary. Egypt, Iraq and Lebanon stayed away over the Suez Crisis. Each empty place was a statement about a war.

South Africa ran a system of racial segregation called *apartheid*. Its sports teams were chosen by race. The IOC barred South Africa from the 1964 Games and expelled it in 1970. In 1976, more than twenty countries, most of them in Africa, left the Montreal Games. They protested a New Zealand rugby tour of South Africa. South Africa returned to the Games in 1992.

In December 1979, the Soviet Union invaded Afghanistan. President Jimmy Carter called for a boycott of the 1980 Moscow Games. The U.S. Olympic Committee voted to stay home, along with dozens of other countries. In 1984, the Soviet Union and more than a dozen allies stayed away from Los Angeles. Romania broke with its allies and came.

words.d: South Africa's system of racial segregation, which kept its teams out of the Olympics from 1964 to 1992
the long rivalry between the United States and the Soviet Union after 1945
a group of countries that act together

review.q: Which statement about Jim Thorpe is correct?
choices: He lost his 1912 medals under the amateur rule.
review.why: Thorpe's 1912 medals were taken in 1913 because he had been paid for baseball.

review.q: What does a boycott of the Games use to send its message?
choices: an empty place in the parade
review.why: A boycott is a refusal to take part, so the missing team is the message.

review.q: Which Games did the Soviet Union and its allies boycott?
review.why: The Soviet Union and more than a dozen allies stayed away from Los Angeles in 1984.

review.q: What is the link between Chicago and the 1904 Games?
choices: Chicago won the vote, but they moved to St. Louis.
Chicago founded the IOC that year.
review.why: Chicago was chosen first, then the Games moved to St. Louis to join the World's Fair.

chapters.title: Title IX and a New Door
chapters.bigQuestion: How did a 1972 education law that never names sports change who gets a place on a school team?

story.title: One Bulletin Board, Two Papers
story.kicker: A federal law and a new team list hang side by side outside an Illinois gym.
paragraphs: Winter, 2022. A bulletin board hangs outside a high school gym in Illinois. Two papers are pinned to it. One is a printed page with a single long sentence from a federal law. The other is a team list with the words Girls Wrestling at the top.

The law is Title IX of the Education Amendments of 1972. President Richard Nixon signed it on June 23, 1972. It is 37 words long. It says no person shall be shut out of an education program because of sex, if that program gets federal money. It does not use the word sport.

The team list is newer. The Illinois High School Association, or IHSA, was founded in 1900. Its first boys wrestling state champions were crowned in 1937. For the 2021–22 season, the IHSA added a girls wrestling state series. The first girls state finals were held in 2022.

Eighty-five years passed between the first boys wrestling champions and the first girls finals. Fifty years passed between the law and the new list. A student reading both papers might wonder what happened in between. The answer runs through Congress, federal rules, courts and school boards.

This chapter follows that path. It starts before 1972, when few girls had school teams at all. Along the way it meets lawmakers, a federal agency, the Supreme Court and a college that lost in court. It ends with the first IHSA girls wrestling state finals.
story.think: Why might a law that never mentions sports still change who plays on school teams?

lessons.title: One Girl in Twenty-Seven
lessons.mainIdea: Before Title IX, about one high school girl in 27 played on a school team, while millions of boys did.
reading: The National Federation of State High School Associations, or *NFHS*, counts school athletes each year. In the 1971–72 school year, it counted about 294,000 girls on high school teams. It counted about 3.67 million boys. That means about one girl in 27 played a school sport.

Many states had no state tournaments for girls at all. Some leaders of girls' physical education in the early 1900s opposed hard competition for girls. They favored *play days*, where girls from several schools mixed together on teams. Iowa was a known exception. It held a girls' state basketball tournament from the 1920s.

The numbers changed quickly after the law. In 1972–73, the NFHS counted about 817,000 girls. By 2018–19, the count reached about 3.4 million. A count taken every year lets historians see a change that a single story cannot show.

words.d: the National Federation of State High School Associations, which counts high school athletes each year
an event where girls from several schools mixed on shared teams instead of competing school against school

look.title: High School Athletes, Then and Later
look.cite: NFHS, High School Athletics Participation Survey
look.prompt: About how many times more girls played in 2018–19 than in 1971–72?

check.q: About how many high school girls played school sports in 1971–72?
check.why: The NFHS counted about 294,000 girls in 1971–72.

check.q: What was a play day?
choices: an event where girls from several schools mixed on shared teams
a day off from school sports
check.why: Play days mixed girls from different schools instead of setting school against school.

check.q: Which state held a girls' state basketball tournament long before 1972?
check.why: Iowa held a girls' state basketball tournament from the 1920s.

lessons.title: College Women Organize
lessons.mainIdea: Women's college sport was run by women's own body, the AIAW, from 1971 until the NCAA took over women's championships in 1981–82.
reading: The *NCAA*, the National Collegiate Athletic Association, was formed in 1906. For most of the 1900s, it held championships only for men. Women's college teams had to build their own institution.

In 1971, women physical educators founded the *AIAW*, the Association for Intercollegiate Athletics for Women. It ran national championships for college women. Its first basketball champion, in 1972, was Immaculata College in Pennsylvania. By the late 1970s, the AIAW had hundreds of member schools.

In the 1981–82 school year, the NCAA began its own women's championships. Many schools moved their women's teams to the NCAA. The AIAW lost members and money. It closed in 1982. Some historians say women gained money and attention, but lost women's control of women's sport.

words.d: the National Collegiate Athletic Association, which runs college sports; formed in 1906
the Association for Intercollegiate Athletics for Women, which ran women's college championships from 1971 to 1982
an organization with its own rules, leaders and records that lasts over time

look.title: Two Bodies, One Season
look.text: In 1981–82, a college women's basketball team could enter the AIAW tournament or the new NCAA tournament. The AIAW was run by women. The NCAA was larger and had television deals for men's sport. Many schools chose the NCAA.
look.prompt: What might a school gain by choosing the NCAA? What might women coaches and leaders lose?

check.q: When was the AIAW founded?
check.why: Women physical educators founded the AIAW in 1971.

check.q: Which school won the AIAW's first basketball championship in 1972?
check.why: Immaculata College in Pennsylvania won in 1972.

check.q: What happened to the AIAW after the NCAA began women's championships?
choices: It lost members and closed in 1982.
check.why: Schools moved to the NCAA, and the AIAW closed in 1982.

lessons.title: The Sentence Itself
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX is one sentence that bans sex discrimination in any education program that receives federal money.
reading: *Title IX* is one part of a larger law, the Education Amendments of 1972. A title is a numbered section of a long law. Title IX has one main sentence. That sentence is 37 words long.

The sentence names three harms. A person may not be excluded from a program because of sex. A person may not be denied its benefits. A person may not be treated unfairly, or face *discrimination*, under it. The rule covers any education program that receives federal money.

Most public schools and many private colleges receive *federal financial assistance*. That is money from the national government, such as grants or student aid. So the rule reaches most American schools. School sports teams are part of an education program, even though the sentence never names them.

words.d: the part of the Education Amendments of 1972 that bans sex discrimination in federally funded education
treating a person unfairly because of who they are, such as their sex or race
money a school receives from the national government

look.title: The Text of Title IX
look.text: No person in the United States shall, on the basis of sex, be excluded from participation in, be denied the benefits of, or be subjected to discrimination under any education program or activity receiving Federal financial assistance.
look.cite: Title IX, Education Amendments of 1972, 20 U.S.C. § 1681(a)
look.prompt: Find the three things the law says may not happen to a person. Which one fits a girl with no team to join?

check.q: Title IX is part of which law?
check.why: Title IX is one section of the Education Amendments of 1972.

check.q: What programs does Title IX cover?
choices: education programs that receive federal money
check.why: The sentence covers any education program or activity receiving federal financial assistance.

check.q: Does the sentence of Title IX use the word sport?
check.why: The sentence speaks of education programs. Sports are covered because they are part of those programs.

lessons.title: Who Wrote It
lessons.mainIdea: Members of Congress Edith Green, Patsy Mink and Birch Bayh moved Title IX into law, and President Nixon signed it on June 23, 1972.
reading: In 1970, Representative *Edith Green* of Oregon held hearings in Congress on unfair treatment of women in education. Bernice Sandler, a researcher, helped gather the evidence. Sandler had filed complaints against many universities that same year. The hearings filled a thick public record.

*Patsy Mink* of Hawaii helped write the law in the House. In 1965, she had become the first woman of color elected to Congress. In the Senate, Birch Bayh of Indiana sponsored Title IX. A *sponsor* is the lawmaker who formally brings a bill forward.
President Richard Nixon signed the Education Amendments on June 23, 1972. Patsy Mink died in 2002. That same year, Congress renamed Title IX the Patsy T. Mink Equal Opportunity in Education Act.

words.d: Oregon member of Congress who held 1970 hearings on sex discrimination in education
Hawaii member of Congress who helped write Title IX; the law was renamed for her in 2002
the lawmaker who formally brings a bill forward

look.title: From Hearings to a New Name
look.cite: Congressional Record; Public Law 92-318 (1972); Public Law 107-255 (2002)
look.prompt: How many years after it was signed was the law renamed?

check.q: Who signed Title IX into law?
check.why: Nixon signed the Education Amendments on June 23, 1972.

check.q: Who held hearings on sex discrimination in education in 1970?
check.why: Representative Edith Green of Oregon held the 1970 hearings.

check.q: What happened to Title IX's name in 2002?
choices: It was renamed for Birch Bayh.
It was renamed the Amateur Sports Act.
It was renamed for Patsy Mink.
check.why: After Patsy Mink died in 2002, Congress renamed the law for her.

lessons.title: Sport Inside a School Law
lessons.mainIdea: Title IX reached sports because school teams are education programs, and the same 1972 law also created college grants.
reading: The Education Amendments of 1972 covered many parts of schooling. The same law created Basic Educational Opportunity Grants. These college grants were renamed Pell Grants in 1980. Title IX was only one section of the law.

Title IX first mattered for admissions, hiring and classes. Some colleges had limited how many women they admitted. Some graduate programs turned women away. The law made those limits illegal in federally funded schools.

School sports were soon pulled in. A school team is an *extracurricular* program, meaning an activity outside regular classes. It still belongs to the school. If a school ran teams for boys only, it was offering a program that girls could not join. That question, in thousands of schools, made Title IX a sports law.

words.d: a school activity that happens outside regular classes, such as a team or club
the federal law that included Title IX and created new college grants

look.title: Is a Team Part of School?
look.text: A public high school gets federal money for reading programs. The same school runs a basketball team for boys and none for girls. The team practices in the school gym, wears school colors and has a coach paid by the school.
look.prompt: Using the words of Title IX, explain why the team counts as part of the school's education program.

check.q: What else did the Education Amendments of 1972 create?
choices: college grants later called Pell Grants
check.why: The 1972 law created Basic Educational Opportunity Grants, renamed Pell Grants in 1980.

check.q: What does extracurricular mean?
check.why: Extracurricular programs, like teams, happen outside class but belong to the school.

check.q: Why do school teams fall under Title IX?
choices: Teams receive money from the IOC.
Teams are part of a school's education program.
check.why: A school team is a school program, and the law covers federally funded school programs.

lessons.title: The 1975 Regulations
lessons.mainIdea: Federal regulations issued in 1975 explained how Title IX applied to sports and gave high schools and colleges until 1978 to comply.
reading: A law often needs *regulations*. These are detailed rules written by a government agency to carry out a law. For Title IX, the agency was the Department of Health, Education, and Welfare, called HEW.

In 1974, Senator John Tower of Texas proposed exempting sports that earned money, such as college football. His amendment failed. Congress instead passed the Javits Amendment, named for Senator Jacob Javits of New York. It told HEW to write sports rules that considered the nature of particular sports.

HEW's Title IX regulations took effect on July 21, 1975. Elementary schools had one year to *comply*, or follow the rules. High schools and colleges had three years, until 1978. The Department of Education was created in 1979. Its Office for Civil Rights now enforces Title IX.

words.d: a detailed rule written by a government agency to carry out a law
to follow a law or rule
a change proposed or made to a bill or law

look.title: Two Amendments in 1974
look.text: The Tower Amendment would have left sports that earn money, like college football, outside Title IX. The Javits Amendment kept all sports inside the law but asked for rules that fit the nature of each sport. Congress rejected the first and passed the second.
look.prompt: How would school sports be different today if the Tower Amendment had passed?

check.q: What did the Tower Amendment try to do?
choices: exempt sports that earned money from Title IX
check.why: Senator Tower's 1974 amendment tried to exempt revenue sports. It failed.

check.q: When did HEW's Title IX regulations take effect?
check.why: The regulations took effect on July 21, 1975.

check.q: How long did high schools and colleges have to comply?
check.why: Elementary schools had one year. High schools and colleges had three years, until 1978.

lessons.title: Separate Teams and Contact Sports
lessons.mainIdea: The Title IX regulations allow separate teams for boys and girls, and they list contact sports, such as wrestling, where a girl need not be allowed onto a boys' team.
reading: The regulations allow schools to run *separate teams* for boys and girls. A school with a boys' team and a girls' team in the same sport can keep them apart. The regulations also list what counts as equal opportunity. The list includes equipment, game schedules, travel, coaching, locker rooms and publicity.

What if a school has a team for only one sex? The regulations say girls must usually be allowed to try out. There is an exception for *contact sports*. The regulations name boxing, wrestling, rugby, ice hockey, football and basketball as contact sports.

Under that exception, the federal rule does not require a school to put a girl on a boys' wrestling team. Some states and schools let girls join anyway, and some girls wrestled on boys' teams for years. A girls' division creates a full team of its own. That is why a girls wrestling state series matters.

words.d: a boys' team and a girls' team in the same sport, which Title IX regulations allow
a sport the Title IX regulations name as involving bodily contact, such as wrestling or football
a case where a rule does not apply

look.title: The Contact Sports List
look.text: The regulation says contact sports include boxing, wrestling, rugby, ice hockey, football, basketball, and other sports whose purpose or major activity involves bodily contact.
look.prompt: Why might a separate girls' wrestling team open more doors than a rule about trying out for the boys' team?

check.q: Do the Title IX regulations allow separate teams for boys and girls?
choices: No, all teams must be mixed.
Yes, schools may run separate teams.
check.why: The regulations allow separate teams and list what equal opportunity must include.

check.q: Which sport is on the regulations' contact sports list?
check.why: The list names boxing, wrestling, rugby, ice hockey, football and basketball.

check.q: What does the contact sports exception mean for a school with only a boys' wrestling team?
choices: Federal rules do not require it to let a girl onto that team.
It must let every girl join.
It must move the team to a college.
check.why: Under the exception, the federal rule does not require a girl to be placed on a boys' contact-sport team.

lessons.title: The Three-Part Test
lessons.mainIdea: A 1979 federal policy gave schools three ways to show they offer fair chances to play, and courts later upheld it.
reading: In 1979, HEW issued a *policy interpretation* for college sports. A policy interpretation explains how an agency will read a law. It set out what is now called the three-part test. A school must pass at least one part.

Part one asks whether the share of team spots for women roughly matches the share of women students. This is often called *proportionality*. Part two asks whether the school has a history of adding teams for women. Part three asks whether the school fully meets its women students' interest and ability.

Schools and students have argued about the test in court. In Cohen v. Brown University, decided in 1996, a federal appeals court upheld the test. Brown had cut women's gymnastics and volleyball in 1991. The court ruled that Brown had not met any of the three parts.

words.d: a government explanation of how it will read and enforce a law
a match between the share of team spots for women and the share of women students
the 1979 standard schools can meet in one of three ways to show fair chances to play

look.title: Checking One College
look.text: A college has 1,000 students: 550 women and 450 men. It has 300 team spots: 120 for women and 180 for men. It has not added a women's team in twenty years. A survey shows many women students want a soccer team the college does not have.
look.prompt: Check each part of the test. Does this college pass any of the three?

check.q: What year did HEW issue the three-part test?
check.why: The policy interpretation with the three-part test came in 1979.

check.q: What does proportionality mean in the test?
choices: Women's share of team spots roughly matches their share of students.
Every team has the same number of players.
Boys and girls play on one team.
Each sport gets the same budget.
check.why: Proportionality compares the share of team spots to the share of students.

check.q: What did the court decide in Cohen v. Brown University?
choices: Title IX does not cover colleges.
It upheld the test and ruled Brown had not met it.
check.why: In 1996 a federal appeals court upheld the test and ruled against Brown.

lessons.title: Courts and Congress
lessons.mainIdea: The Supreme Court narrowed Title IX in 1984, Congress restored it in 1988, and a 1992 case let students win money damages.
reading: In Grove City College v. Bell, in 1984, the U.S. Supreme Court read Title IX narrowly. It said the law covered only the part of a school that got the federal money. A college's sports program could escape the law if no federal money went to it directly.

Congress answered with the *Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1988*. It said Title IX covers a whole school if any part of it receives federal money. President Ronald Reagan vetoed the bill. A *veto* is a president's refusal to sign. Congress voted to override the veto in March 1988, and the act became law.

In Franklin v. Gwinnett County Public Schools, in 1992, the Supreme Court ruled that students could sue for money damages under Title IX. That gave the law more force. Each of these steps shows that a law's reach is shaped by courts and Congress long after it passes.

words.d: a president's refusal to sign a bill; Congress can override it with a two-thirds vote in each house
the law that made Title IX cover a whole school if any part receives federal money
money a court orders paid to someone who was harmed

look.title: Title IX After 1972
look.cite: Federal Register (1975, 1979); U.S. Supreme Court reports; Public Law 100-259 (1988)
look.prompt: How many years did Title IX's narrow reading last before Congress restored it?

check.q: What did the Supreme Court decide in Grove City College v. Bell?
choices: Title IX covered every school club.
Title IX covered only the part of a school that got federal money.
check.why: In 1984 the Court read the law to cover only the funded part of a school.

check.q: How did the Civil Rights Restoration Act become law?
check.why: Reagan vetoed the bill, and Congress overrode the veto in March 1988.

check.q: What did Franklin v. Gwinnett County decide in 1992?
choices: Students could sue for money damages under Title IX.
check.why: The 1992 ruling let students win money damages under Title IX.

lessons.title: The IHSA and Boys Wrestling
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA, founded in 1900, crowned its first boys wrestling state champions in 1937.
reading: The *Illinois High School Association*, or IHSA, was founded in 1900. It is the body that sets rules and runs state tournaments for Illinois high schools. Its member schools agree to follow its rules on who may play and when.

A *state series* is the IHSA's chain of tournaments that ends in a state final. Wrestling joined early. The IHSA crowned its first boys wrestling state champions in 1937. For decades, that series was for boys only.

In the 1970s, after Title IX and its regulations, the IHSA added state tournaments for girls, sport by sport. Wrestling was not among them then. Girls who wanted to wrestle could sometimes join boys' teams, but they had no state series of their own.

words.d: the body, founded in 1900, that runs rules and state tournaments for Illinois high schools
the chain of IHSA tournaments that ends in a state final

look.title: Illinois Dates on One Chart
look.prompt: How many years passed between the first boys wrestling champions and the first girls finals?

check.q: When was the IHSA founded?
check.why: The IHSA was founded in 1900.

check.q: When did the IHSA crown its first boys wrestling state champions?
check.why: The first IHSA boys wrestling state champions were crowned in 1937.

check.q: What is a state series?
choices: the IHSA's chain of tournaments that ends in a state final
check.why: A state series is the IHSA tournament path that leads to a state final.

lessons.title: A Girls Series in 2022
lessons.mainIdea: The IHSA added girls wrestling for the 2021–22 season and held the first girls state finals in 2022.
reading: In the late 1990s, a few states began state tournaments for girls' wrestling. Hawaii and Texas were among the first. More states followed over the next twenty years. Women's wrestling joined the Olympic Games at Athens in 2004, which drew more attention to the sport.

Illinois added girls wrestling as an IHSA sport for the 2021–22 season. The first girls wrestling state finals were held in 2022. That was 85 years after the first boys champions, and 50 years after Title IX. The IHSA now keeps girls wrestling champions in its own records, beside the boys' list that began in 1937.

A new state series is an *institutional* change. It means a written rule, a place in the IHSA calendar, officials and a record book. Girls who wrestled before 2022 had to fit inside a boys' program. After 2022, they had a program built for them.

words.d: a separate group within a tournament, such as a girls' division
about an organization's rules, records and structure, not one person's choice

look.title: What a New Series Adds
look.text: Before 2022, an Illinois girl who wrestled joined a boys' team and competed in the boys' state series. After 2022, she could enter a girls state series with its own brackets, its own champions and its own line in the IHSA record book.
look.prompt: Name two things a girls' division gives wrestlers that a place on a boys' team did not.

check.q: When did Illinois hold its first girls wrestling state finals?
check.why: The IHSA added girls wrestling for 2021–22, and the first finals were held in 2022.

check.q: When did women's wrestling join the Olympic Games?
check.why: Women's wrestling was added at the Athens Games in 2004.

check.q: Why is a new state series an institutional change?
choices: It depends on one coach's choice.
It creates a written rule, a calendar place, officials and a record book.
check.why: An institution has rules, records and structure. A state series adds all of these.

review.q: What did the 1971–72 NFHS count show?
choices: About one girl in 27 played a high school sport.
Girls and boys played in equal numbers.
review.why: About 294,000 girls and 3.67 million boys played in 1971–72.

review.q: Which body ran women's college championships before the NCAA took them over?
review.why: The AIAW ran women's college championships from 1971 until it closed in 1982.

review.q: What is the key phrase that brings a school under Title IX?
review.why: Title IX covers education programs receiving federal financial assistance.

review.q: How is a law different from a regulation?
choices: A regulation is passed by Congress; a law is written by an agency.
A regulation is a court case.
Congress passes a law; an agency writes regulations to carry it out.
review.why: Congress passed Title IX in 1972. HEW wrote the 1975 regulations to carry it out.

review.q: Which lawmaker helped write Title IX and later had it renamed for her?
review.why: Congress renamed the law for Patsy Mink in 2002.

review.q: Why did Congress pass the Civil Rights Restoration Act of 1988?
choices: to answer the Grove City College ruling
to add wrestling to the Olympics
review.why: The 1984 Grove City ruling narrowed Title IX. The 1988 act restored its reach to whole schools.

review.q: Why does the contact sports exception matter for girls' wrestling?
choices: It requires mixed teams in every sport.
It means federal rules do not require girls to be put on boys' wrestling teams.
review.why: Wrestling is on the contact sports list, so a separate girls' division opens a door the exception leaves closed.

review.q: Which pair of Illinois dates is correct?
choices: boys wrestling champions 1937; girls wrestling finals 2022
review.why: The IHSA crowned its first boys wrestling champions in 1937 and held its first girls finals in 2022.
